topics.title: What is a period, and why does it happen?
topics.caption: Every month, the uterus builds a soft, cosy lining.

topics.title: Four phases: a month-long moon story
topics.caption: Period, egg growing, egg release, lining waits.

topics.title: Hormones: your body’s messengers
topics.caption: Oestrogen and progesterone rise and fall like tides.

topics.title: How long is a cycle? Every body differs
topics.caption: For teens, 21 to 45 days is common.

topics.title: Tracking your cycle like a pro
topics.caption: A simple diary helps you notice your own rhythm.

pause_and_think.prompt: Which phase comes right after the period?
pause_and_think.explanation: After the period, the follicular phase begins and a new egg starts growing in the ovary.

pause_and_think.prompt: Which hormone helps build the cosy lining?
pause_and_think.explanation: Oestrogen rises in the first half and builds the lining. Progesterone keeps it ready in the second half.

pause_and_think.prompt: For most teens, how long is one cycle?
pause_and_think.explanation: For teens, 21 to 45 days is common while the body finds its rhythm.

discover_cards.label: SCIENCE FACT
discover_cards.front: A girl is born with all the eggs she will ever have.
discover_cards.back: That’s about 1 to 2 million at birth! Only around 400 are ever released in a lifetime.

discover_cards.label: MYTH OR FACT?
discover_cards.front: “You shouldn’t exercise or play during your period.”
discover_cards.back: Gentle movement often eases cramps. Dance, play, stretch, whatever feels good for you.

discover_cards.label: GIGI WONDERS
discover_cards.front: Why is it called a cycle?
discover_cards.back: Because it goes round and round and starts again, a bit like the moon’s phases. That’s why your Play activity was a moon!

reflect.journal_prompt: Before today I thought periods were… Now I know…

quick_check.prompt: The period is when…
quick_check.explanation: Yes, the lining gently leaves the body. That’s day 1 of a new cycle.

quick_check.prompt: Every girl’s cycle is exactly 28 days.
quick_check.explanation: False! Cycles vary, especially in the first couple of years.

quick_check.prompt: Which phase comes right after the egg is released?
quick_check.explanation: The luteal phase: the lining waits, just in case.

reflect.summary: 3 things you know now: periods are part of a cycle, cycles vary, and tracking helps.

topics.title: Menarche: your very first period
topics.caption: Most girls get their first period between 9 and 15.

topics.title: Puberty: the big upgrade
topics.caption: Breasts, body hair, height and shape change in their own order.

topics.title: Skin, sweat and smart care
topics.caption: Hormones wake up sweat and oil glands. A daily wash helps.

topics.title: Mood swings: oestrogen and progesterone at work
topics.caption: When hormones shift, feelings can shift too.

topics.title: Irregular periods in the first years
topics.caption: It can take 1 to 2 years for cycles to settle.

pause_and_think.prompt: Which is often one of the first signs of puberty?
pause_and_think.explanation: Breast buds often appear a year or two before the first period.

pause_and_think.prompt: Why can moods swing during puberty?

options.text: Hormones like oestrogen and progesterone are changing

pause_and_think.explanation: Changing hormone levels affect feelings. It’s normal, and talking helps.

pause_and_think.prompt: Your period skips a month in the first year. That’s…

options.text: Usually normal while the body settles

pause_and_think.explanation: Cycles often take 1 to 2 years to settle. If you’re worried, tell a grown-up.

discover_cards.label: SCIENCE FACT
discover_cards.front: Most girls in India get their first period around 12 or 13.
discover_cards.back: But anywhere from 9 to 15 is normal. Your body has its own clock.

discover_cards.label: MYTH OR FACT?
discover_cards.front: “Once your periods start, you stop growing taller.”
discover_cards.back: Growth slows down, but most girls still grow a few more centimetres after their first period.

discover_cards.label: GIGI WONDERS
discover_cards.front: Why do I sweat more now?
discover_cards.back: Puberty wakes up special sweat glands under the arms. A daily bath and fresh clothes keep you feeling fresh.

reflect.journal_prompt: Which change am I most curious (or nervous) about, and why?
sentence_starters: One thing that feels new is…
I’d like to ask Mom about…

quick_check.prompt: What is menarche?
quick_check.explanation: Menarche is the first period, a big milestone of puberty.

quick_check.prompt: Every girl goes through puberty changes in the same order.
quick_check.explanation: False! The order and timing are different for everyone.

quick_check.prompt: Which two hormones can affect your mood?
quick_check.explanation: Oestrogen and progesterone rise and fall through the cycle.

reflect.summary: 3 things you know now: menarche is your first period, puberty has its own order for everyone, and mood swings are hormones at work.

topics.title: Light, medium, heavy: types of flow
topics.caption: Flow often changes from day to day.

topics.title: How much is normal?
topics.caption: Usually about 2 to 3 tablespoons over a whole period.

topics.title: Why periods change: stress, weight, hormones
topics.caption: Exams, illness, big weight changes and hormones can shift your cycle.

topics.title: Myths and facts
topics.caption: Let’s bust a few myths you may have heard.

pause_and_think.prompt: Day 1 is heavy and day 5 is very light. Is that normal?

options.text: Yes, flow changes day to day
No, flow should be the same every day

pause_and_think.explanation: Most periods start heavier and get lighter.

pause_and_think.prompt: Which is a sign to tell a grown-up?

options.text: Soaking a pad every 1 to 2 hours
A light flow on the last day

pause_and_think.explanation: Soaking through a pad every 1 to 2 hours, or bleeding more than 7 days, is worth checking with a doctor.

pause_and_think.prompt: Which can make a period come late?
pause_and_think.explanation: Stress hormones can delay ovulation, so the period comes later.

discover_cards.label: SCIENCE FACT
discover_cards.front: Period blood is not “dirty” blood.
discover_cards.back: It’s blood plus the soft uterus lining, and it’s just as clean as blood from a scraped knee.

discover_cards.label: MYTH OR FACT?
discover_cards.front: “During your period you’ll spoil pickle if you touch it.”
discover_cards.back: Periods can’t spoil food. This belief has no science behind it at all.

discover_cards.label: GIGI WONDERS
discover_cards.front: Why are there sometimes small clots?
discover_cards.back: Small jelly-like clots on heavy days are common. Clots bigger than a ₹5 coin are worth mentioning to a doctor.

reflect.journal_prompt: A myth I heard about periods was… and the truth is…

quick_check.prompt: Which is a light flow?

options.text: A few spots on the pad

quick_check.explanation: A few spots is light. Soaking a pad hourly is very heavy.

quick_check.prompt: Stress can change when your period comes.
quick_check.explanation: True. Stress hormones can delay a period.

quick_check.prompt: Bleeding for more than how many days is worth checking?
quick_check.explanation: More than 7 days is a reason to see a doctor.

reflect.summary: 3 things you know now: flow changes day to day, stress can shift your cycle, and myths are just myths.

topics.title: Why period care keeps your whole body healthy
topics.caption: Clean habits keep germs away and keep you comfortable.

topics.title: Infections: vaginitis and UTIs
topics.caption: Germs can cause itching or burning. Simple habits prevent most of them.

topics.title: Front to back, and other smart habits
topics.caption: Always wipe front to back, and change pads on time.

topics.title: Discomfort and odour: what’s normal
topics.caption: A mild smell is normal. Changing on time keeps you fresh.

pause_and_think.prompt: How often should you change a pad?

options.text: Every 4 to 6 hours, sooner if full

pause_and_think.explanation: Every 4 to 6 hours keeps germs and smell away.

pause_and_think.prompt: Which way should you wipe?
pause_and_think.explanation: Front to back keeps germs from the back passage away from the vagina and urinary opening.

pause_and_think.prompt: Your period has a mild smell. What helps?

options.text: Change on time and wash outside with plain water

pause_and_think.explanation: The vagina cleans itself. Plain water outside is enough; scented products irritate.

discover_cards.label: SCIENCE FACT
discover_cards.front: The vagina cleans itself!
discover_cards.back: Good bacteria called lactobacilli keep it healthy. Plain water on the outside is all you need.

discover_cards.label: MYTH OR FACT?
discover_cards.front: “You shouldn’t bathe or wash your hair during your period.”
discover_cards.back: A warm bath keeps you fresh and can even ease cramps.

discover_cards.label: GIGI WONDERS
discover_cards.front: Why does period blood smell a little?
discover_cards.back: When blood meets air it gets a mild smell. Changing on time keeps it fresh. A strong fishy smell with itching is a reason to tell a grown-up.

reflect.journal_prompt: My fresh-and-comfy plan for my next period is…

quick_check.prompt: How often should you change a pad?
quick_check.explanation: Every 4 to 6 hours, sooner if it’s full.

quick_check.prompt: Scented sprays are good for the vagina.
quick_check.explanation: False. They can irritate and upset its balance.

quick_check.prompt: A urinary tract infection (UTI) can cause…
quick_check.explanation: Burning or needing to pee often are signs. Tell a grown-up.

reflect.summary: 3 things you know now: change on time, wipe front to back, and plain water is enough.

topics.title: Sanitary pads: the classic choice
topics.caption: Pads stick to your underwear and come in many sizes.

topics.title: Tampons: worn inside
topics.caption: A tampon is worn inside and changed every 4 to 8 hours.

topics.title: Menstrual cups: reusable and eco
topics.caption: A soft silicone cup collects flow and can last for years.

topics.title: Cloth pads and period underwear
topics.caption: Washable options cut down on waste.

topics.title: Pros and cons: what suits you?
topics.caption: There’s no single best product, only the best one for you.

pause_and_think.prompt: How often should a tampon be changed?
pause_and_think.explanation: Never leave a tampon in for more than 8 hours.

pause_and_think.prompt: Which products can be reused?
pause_and_think.explanation: Cups and cloth pads can be washed and used again.

pause_and_think.prompt: Which product is best for everyone?
pause_and_think.explanation: Comfort, activity, budget and the planet all matter. Try and decide.

discover_cards.label: SCIENCE FACT
discover_cards.front: One girl may use 10,000 or more disposable pads in her lifetime.
discover_cards.back: Most contain plastic that can take hundreds of years to break down. Reusables help cut that waste.

discover_cards.label: MYTH OR FACT?
discover_cards.front: “Girls can’t use tampons or cups until they’re grown up.”
discover_cards.back: Teens can use them too, when they feel ready and know how. Many girls start with pads first.

discover_cards.label: GIGI WONDERS
discover_cards.front: What is period underwear?
discover_cards.back: Underwear with soft absorbent layers built in. Wear, rinse, wash and reuse.

reflect.journal_prompt: If I could design my dream period product, it would…
sentence_starters: The product I’d try first is…

quick_check.prompt: Which product is worn inside the body?
quick_check.explanation: Tampons (and cups) are worn inside.

quick_check.prompt: Reusable products help reduce waste.
quick_check.explanation: True! A cup or cloth pad replaces hundreds of disposables.

quick_check.prompt: A tampon should never stay in longer than…
quick_check.explanation: 8 hours at most, to stay safe.

reflect.summary: 3 things you know now: there’s a product for every need, reusables cut waste, and changing on time keeps you safe.

topics.title: Using a pad, step by step
topics.caption: Peel, stick, and change every 4 to 6 hours.

topics.title: Tampons and cups: using them safely
topics.caption: Clean hands first, always. Read the leaflet with a grown-up.

topics.title: Caring for cloth pads
topics.caption: Rinse in cold water, wash with soap, dry in the sun.

topics.title: Wrap it, bin it, never flush it

topics.title: Cleaning a cup between periods

pause_and_think.prompt: What’s the first step before changing any product?
pause_and_think.explanation: Clean hands keep germs away from your body.

pause_and_think.prompt: Where should cloth pads dry?
pause_and_think.explanation: Sunlight helps kill germs. There’s nothing to hide!

pause_and_think.prompt: Can you flush a used pad down the toilet?

options.text: No, wrap it and bin it

pause_and_think.explanation: Pads block pipes and harm rivers. Wrap and bin.

discover_cards.label: SCIENCE FACT
discover_cards.front: Wrapping used pads keeps sanitation workers safe.
discover_cards.back: India’s waste rules ask us to wrap sanitary waste in paper or a pouch before it goes in the bin.

discover_cards.label: MYTH OR FACT?
discover_cards.front: “It’s fine to flush a pad if you’re in a hurry.”
discover_cards.back: Pads swell up and block pipes. Always wrap and bin, even in a hurry.

discover_cards.label: GIGI WONDERS
discover_cards.front: What if there’s no bin in the toilet?
discover_cards.back: Wrap it well, pop it in a small disposal bag from your pouch, and bin it later.

reflect.journal_prompt: What would make changing at school easier for me?

quick_check.prompt: Pads can be flushed.
quick_check.explanation: False! Wrap and bin.

quick_check.prompt: Cloth pads should dry…
quick_check.explanation: Sunlight helps kill germs.

reflect.summary: 3 things you know now: clean hands first, wrap and bin, and sunshine for cloth pads.

topics.title: What is menstrual discomfort?
topics.caption: Many girls feel some discomfort around their period. You’re not alone.

topics.title: Cramps, bloating, back pain and tiredness
topics.caption: Cramps feel like a squeeze in the lower tummy.

topics.title: Why it happens: hormones and squeezes
topics.caption: Chemicals called prostaglandins make the uterus squeeze to let the lining out.

topics.title: Why some girls feel more than others
topics.caption: Genes, flow, stress, sleep and activity all play a part.

pause_and_think.prompt: Where are cramps usually felt?

options.text: Lower tummy, sometimes back and thighs

pause_and_think.explanation: The uterus sits low in the tummy, so that’s where the squeeze is felt.

pause_and_think.prompt: What makes the uterus squeeze?
pause_and_think.explanation: Prostaglandins rise at the start of a period. More of them can mean stronger cramps.

pause_and_think.prompt: Your friend’s cramps are stronger than yours. That means…
pause_and_think.explanation: Discomfort varies a lot. Be kind to her, and to yourself.

discover_cards.label: SCIENCE FACT
discover_cards.front: More than half of teen girls get period cramps.
discover_cards.back: Discomfort is common, and there are many ways to ease it.

discover_cards.label: MYTH OR FACT?
discover_cards.front: “Pain that makes you miss school every month is just normal.”
discover_cards.back: Strong pain is worth checking with a doctor. You don’t have to just put up with it.

discover_cards.label: GIGI WONDERS
discover_cards.front: Why do I feel puffy before my period?
discover_cards.back: Hormones make the body hold a bit more water. Drinking water and fewer salty snacks can help.

reflect.journal_prompt: When I feel discomfort, the thing that helps me most is… (or I’ll try…)

quick_check.prompt: What can ease cramps?
quick_check.explanation: Warmth relaxes the muscles.

quick_check.prompt: Every girl feels the same amount of discomfort.
quick_check.explanation: False. It varies a lot from girl to girl.

quick_check.prompt: When should you tell a grown-up?

options.text: Pain stops you from going to school

quick_check.explanation: Strong pain deserves a doctor’s help.

reflect.summary: 3 things you know now: discomfort is common, warmth, movement and rest help, and strong pain needs a doctor.

topics.title: What’s happening inside: a quick tour
topics.caption: The uterus, ovaries and hormones work as a team.

topics.title: Endometriosis: tissue in the wrong place
topics.caption: Tissue like the lining grows outside the uterus and can cause strong pain.

topics.title: PCOS: when hormones get out of balance
topics.caption: It can cause irregular periods, acne or extra hair.

topics.title: Menorrhagia: very heavy bleeding
topics.caption: Soaking a pad every 1 to 2 hours is a reason to see a doctor.

topics.title: Amenorrhea: when periods don’t come
topics.caption: No period by 15, or missing 3 in a row, is worth checking.

pause_and_think.prompt: Strong period pain from endometriosis is…

options.text: A reason to see a doctor

pause_and_think.explanation: Doctors can find the cause and help. Never suffer in silence.

pause_and_think.prompt: Which can be a sign of PCOS?

options.text: Periods very far apart, plus acne or extra hair

pause_and_think.explanation: PCOS is common and can be managed with a doctor’s help.

pause_and_think.prompt: If periods haven’t started by 15, you should…

options.text: Tell a grown-up and see a doctor

pause_and_think.explanation: A check-up gives answers, and usually peace of mind.

discover_cards.label: SCIENCE FACT
discover_cards.front: About 1 in 10 girls and women have PCOS.
discover_cards.back: It’s common, and with the right care, girls with PCOS live full, happy lives.

discover_cards.label: MYTH OR FACT?
discover_cards.front: “If you have a menstrual disorder, you did something wrong.”
discover_cards.back: These conditions are nobody’s fault. Doctors can help you feel better.

discover_cards.label: GIGI WONDERS
discover_cards.front: What happens at a doctor’s check-up?
discover_cards.back: The doctor asks questions, may gently press on your tummy, and sometimes does an ultrasound scan. Mom or a trusted adult can stay with you.

reflect.journal_prompt: If I ever felt something wasn’t right with my period, I would tell…

quick_check.prompt: Menorrhagia means…
quick_check.explanation: Very heavy or long bleeding.

quick_check.prompt: Menstrual disorders are always the girl’s fault.
quick_check.explanation: False. They’re nobody’s fault.

quick_check.prompt: Amenorrhea means…
quick_check.explanation: Periods that don’t start, or stop.

reflect.summary: 3 things you know now: strong pain isn’t something to hide, very heavy or missing periods need a doctor, and it’s never your fault.

topics.title: What is a vaginal infection?
topics.caption: Sometimes the balance of good and bad germs changes.

topics.title: Bacterial vaginosis: signs to notice
topics.caption: A thin grey-white discharge with a fishy smell.

topics.title: Yeast infections: itchy and uncomfortable
topics.caption: Thick white discharge and itching.

topics.title: What to do if you notice symptoms
topics.caption: Tell a grown-up and see a doctor. Don’t treat it yourself.

pause_and_think.explanation: Healthy discharge is the vagina’s way of cleaning itself.

pause_and_think.prompt: Which is a sign of a yeast infection?

options.text: Tell a grown-up and see a doctor

discover_cards.label: GIGI WONDERS

quick_check.prompt: Infections are common and can be treated.

quick_check.prompt: If you notice itching, you should…

topics.title: What is bullying?
topics.caption: Bullying is hurting someone again and again, on purpose.

topics.title: Cyberbullying: when it happens online
topics.caption: Mean messages, edited photos or leaving someone out of a group chat.

topics.title: How bullying hurts
topics.caption: It can affect sleep, mood, marks and confidence.

topics.title: Be an upstander: safe ways to help

discover_cards.label: GIGI WONDERS

quick_check.prompt: Forwarding a mean meme is a way of joining in.

quick_check.prompt: An upstander…

options.text: Helps safely and tells an adult

topics.title: What does abuse mean?
topics.caption: Abuse is when someone hurts a child on purpose, in their body or their feelings.

topics.title: Physical, emotional and sexual abuse
topics.caption: Hitting, scaring, or touching private parts are never okay.

topics.title: Noticing the signs
topics.caption: Feeling scared, confused or asked to keep a secret are signs to tell.

topics.title: Healthy boundaries and consent
topics.caption: You can say no to any touch, even from someone you know.

topics.title: How to tell and report
topics.caption: Keep telling until someone helps. Call 1098 or 112.

pause_and_think.prompt: Your private parts are the parts covered by…
pause_and_think.explanation: The swimsuit rule: nobody should touch or ask to see these parts, except a doctor checking you with a parent there, or to keep you clean and healthy when you are little.

pause_and_think.prompt: Someone asks you to keep a touch secret. You should…
pause_and_think.explanation: Touch should never be a secret. Telling is always right.

pause_and_think.prompt: If the first adult doesn’t listen, you…
pause_and_think.explanation: Tell another trusted adult, or call 1098. You deserve to be heard.

discover_cards.label: SCIENCE FACT
discover_cards.front: It is never a child’s fault if someone touches them in an unsafe way.

activities.name: Build-a-Cycle Moon
activities.instructions: Tap a petal, then tap its place on the moon. Start at the top right and go round.

slots.label: Period
slots.fact: The cosy lining gently leaves the body. That’s your period!
slots.hint: The cycle starts with the period, at the top right.

slots.label: Egg growing
slots.fact: A new egg grows inside the ovary, and a fresh lining starts to build.
slots.hint: After the period, something starts to grow.

slots.label: Egg released
slots.fact: The ovary releases the egg. This is called ovulation.
slots.hint: Halfway round, the egg is let go.

slots.label: Lining waiting
slots.fact: The lining waits. If it isn’t needed, the cycle begins again.
slots.hint: Last comes the waiting part, before it all starts again.

config.footnote: Days shown for a 28-day cycle. Every body has its own rhythm.
config.done_line: The moon turns once for every cycle, just like your body.

config.instructions: Every girl travels through puberty in her own order. Tap each stop, read what happens, and stamp your passport.
config.done_line: 8 of 8 stamps. Remember: everyone visits these stops in her own order and her own time.

cards.name: Breast buds
cards.back: Small, tender bumps under the nipples are often the first sign. One side may grow first, that’s okay.
cards.tip: A soft cotton slip or starter bra can feel comfy.

cards.name: Body hair
cards.back: Hair grows under the arms, on the legs and around the private parts.
cards.tip: Removing it is your choice, never a must.

cards.name: Growth spurt
cards.back: You may grow several centimetres in a year. Clothes suddenly feel short!
cards.tip: Good sleep and food help growing bones.

cards.name: New shape
cards.back: Hips widen and the body gets softer curves. Every shape is a healthy shape.

cards.name: Skin and sweat
cards.back: Oil and sweat glands wake up, so pimples and body odour can appear.
cards.tip: Wash your face twice a day and bathe daily.

cards.name: First period
cards.back: Menarche usually comes about 2 years after breast buds start, often between 9 and 15.
cards.tip: Keep a pad in your bag once breast buds appear.

cards.name: Big feelings
cards.back: Oestrogen and progesterone can make feelings go up and down quickly.
cards.tip: Name the feeling, then breathe or talk.

cards.name: Irregular at first
cards.back: Periods can be far apart or close together for the first 1 to 2 years.
cards.tip: Track it in your Diary to spot your rhythm.

config.instructions: Six case files have landed on your desk. Read each clue and crack the case.
config.done_line: You read the clues like a pro. Flow changes, stress can shift it, and heavy or long periods mean tell a grown-up.

cases.scene: Sana sees just a few brownish spots on her pad.
cases.question: What kind of flow is this?
cases.feedback: Light flow. Brown blood is simply older blood, totally normal at the start or end.

cases.scene: Mira changes a well-used pad every 4 to 5 hours.
cases.question: What kind of flow is this?
cases.feedback: Medium flow, and she’s changing on time. Case closed!

cases.scene: Tara soaks through a pad every hour for several hours and feels dizzy.
cases.question: What should Tara do?

options.text: Tell a grown-up and see a doctor

cases.feedback: Very heavy flow with dizziness needs a doctor. Telling a grown-up is the brave, smart move.

cases.scene: Anu’s period came 10 days late during board-exam week.
cases.question: What’s the likely clue?
cases.feedback: Stress can shift the cycle. If it keeps happening, she can check with a doctor.

cases.scene: Ira’s period has now lasted 9 days.
cases.question: What should Ira do?

options.text: Tell a grown-up: more than 7 days is worth checking

cases.feedback: Periods usually last 2 to 7 days. Longer is a good reason to see a doctor.

cases.scene: Neha’s aunt says she must not bathe during her period.
cases.question: Myth or fact?
cases.feedback: Myth busted! A warm bath keeps you fresh and can ease cramps.

config.instructions: Build your care clock! Tap the right time for each habit, and catch the ones to skip.
config.done_line: Daily freshness, on-time changes, a night pad, and no perfumes. That’s a Care Captain routine.

items.text: Bath, and wash outside with plain water
items.explanation: A daily bath keeps you fresh. Water outside is all you need.

items.text: Put on fresh cotton underwear
items.explanation: Cotton lets skin breathe, so germs don’t grow.

items.text: Change my pad (every 4 to 6 hours)
items.explanation: On-time changes stop smell, rashes and germs.

items.text: Wash my hands before and after
items.explanation: Clean hands, clean change.

items.text: Wipe from front to back
items.explanation: Every time you use the toilet, too.

items.text: Wear a fresh, longer pad for the night
items.explanation: Night pads are longer, so you can sleep without worry.

items.text: Spray perfume down there
items.explanation: Scents irritate delicate skin. Skip it!

items.text: Wash inside the vagina with soap
items.explanation: The vagina cleans itself. Soap inside upsets its balance.

items.text: Wear the same pad all day
items.explanation: Germs grow in a used pad. Change every 4 to 6 hours.

config.instructions: Four friends need help choosing a period product. Read about each one and make the match.
config.done_line: Every product has pros and cons. The best one is the one that suits your body, your day and your planet.

cases.scene: Zoya expects her first period soon and wants something simple to start with.
cases.question: What would you suggest?
cases.feedback: Pads are easy and a great first choice. Pros: simple, many sizes. Cons: single use, so more waste.

cases.scene: Diya swims for her school team and has a meet during her period.
cases.question: What could work in the pool?
cases.feedback: Pads don’t work in water. Tampons or cups can, once she’s comfortable and has asked a grown-up.

cases.scene: Meher loves the planet and wants less waste.
cases.question: Which match fits Meher?
cases.feedback: One cup can last years. Pros: less waste, saves money. Cons: needs practice and washing.

cases.scene: Kiara has a 2-hour bus ride on a heavy-flow day.
cases.question: What should she pack?

options.text: A long heavy-flow pad, plus a spare

cases.feedback: Heavy days need higher absorbency, and a spare in the pouch means no worries.

config.instructions: Tap the steps in the right order. Two rounds: changing a pad, then caring for a cloth pad.
config.done_line: Clean hands, wrap and bin, never flush, and sunshine for cloth pads.

rounds.name: Change a pad
steps_in_order: Roll it up in the wrapper or paper
Stick the new pad in place

rounds.name: Care for a cloth pad
steps_in_order: Fold and keep in a clean pouch

config.wrong_hint: Not yet! Think about what has to happen before that.

activities.name: School Day Surprise
activities.instructions: A branching story, then pack your own school pouch.

nodes.text: Maths class, second period. Aanya feels something different… she thinks her period has started!

choices.label: Raise her hand to use the washroom

nodes.text: Zoya smiles: "Happens to all of us! Let’s tell Ms. Kapoor together."
The bell is still 30 minutes away. Aanya feels a bit worried.
nodes.gigi: Your body is never a disturbance. It’s always okay to step out.

nodes.text: Ms. Kapoor nods kindly and lets her go. No questions, no fuss.
"May I use the washroom, please?" The teacher says yes with a smile.
In the washroom, Aanya takes a deep breath. She’s got this.

choices.label: The emergency pouch in her bag

nodes.text: Fresh pad, wrap the used one, bin it, wash hands. Back in class in 5 minutes, feeling proud!
The nurse has pads ready and a kind smile. Next time, a pouch in her bag will make it even easier.

pack.wrong_msg: That one can stay at home.

config.instructions: Gigi’s body map is glowing in 4 places. Tap a spot, then pick the comfort tools that help.
config.done_line: Warmth, movement, water and rest. You know what helps your body feel better.

spots.name: Tummy cramps
spots.tip: Warmth relaxes the squeezing muscles, and gentle movement helps too.

spots.name: Lower back ache
spots.tip: A warm bottle on the back and a cat-cow stretch can ease it.

spots.name: Bloated belly
spots.tip: Water and less salt help your body let go of extra water.

spots.name: Feeling tired
spots.tip: Rest, water and a little fresh air can recharge you.

config.warning: Tell a grown-up if pain stops you from going to school, or if it doesn’t get better. Medicine only with a parent or doctor.

config.instructions: Sort each clue. Is it usually normal, or a sign to tell a grown-up and see a doctor?
config.done_line: You can spot what’s usually normal and what needs a doctor. And remember: you can tell a grown-up about anything.

items.text: Mild cramps on day 1 or 2
items.explanation: Common, and warmth or a stretch helps.

items.text: Cycles of 25 to 40 days in the first year
items.explanation: Normal while your body settles.

items.text: Feeling a bit tired during your period
items.explanation: Common. Rest and water help.

items.text: Pain so strong you miss school every month
items.explanation: This could be endometriosis or something else a doctor can treat.

items.text: Soaking a pad every 1 to 2 hours
items.explanation: That’s menorrhagia, very heavy bleeding. A doctor can help.

items.text: No period by age 15
items.explanation: That’s called primary amenorrhea. A check-up gives answers.

items.text: Periods stop for 3 months after being regular
items.explanation: Worth checking, even if you feel fine.

items.text: Very irregular periods with lots of acne or extra hair
items.explanation: These can be signs of PCOS, which a doctor can manage.

config.instructions: Germs are knocking! Decide which habits shield you and which ones let germs in.
config.done_line: Cotton, on-time changes, front to back and dry skin. And if something itches or smells strange, you tell.

items.text: Cotton underwear
items.explanation: Cotton breathes, so germs can’t settle in.

items.text: Changing pads every 4 to 6 hours
items.explanation: Fresh pads, fewer germs.

items.text: Wiping front to back
items.explanation: Keeps germs from the back passage away.

items.text: Drying well after a bath
items.explanation: Germs love damp places.

items.text: Telling a grown-up about itching
items.explanation: The fastest way to get treated.

items.text: Scented sprays and washes
items.explanation: They upset the good bacteria.

items.text: Sitting in a wet swimsuit for hours
items.explanation: Damp, tight clothes help yeast grow. Change soon after swimming.

items.text: Washing inside the vagina (douching)
items.explanation: It washes away the good bacteria that protect you.

config.instructions: Four moments at school and online. What would an upstander do?
config.done_line: You don’t join in, you include, and you tell. That’s how safe schools are built.

cases.scene: Someone posts a meme making fun of Riya’s teeth. Everyone is sending laughing faces.
cases.question: What would an upstander do?

options.text: Don’t share it, send Riya something kind, tell a teacher

cases.feedback: Not sharing stops it spreading. A kind message and an adult’s help make a big difference.

cases.scene: A group won’t let Ananya sit with them, again and again.
cases.question: What could you do?

options.text: Invite Ananya to sit with you

cases.feedback: Including someone is a quiet, powerful way to stand up.

cases.scene: Someone keeps calling you names and it really hurts.
cases.question: What’s a good step?
cases.feedback: It’s not your fault. Telling isn’t tattling, it’s getting help.

cases.scene: A stranger in a game chat asks for your photo and your school name.
cases.question: What should you do?

options.text: Don’t reply, block, and tell a grown-up

cases.feedback: Never share photos or personal details with strangers online. Block and tell.

config.instructions: Sort each moment calmly. Take your time, there’s no timer here.
config.done_line: Safe touch is never secret. You can say no, and you can always tell.

items.text: A high five from a friend
items.explanation: A friendly touch you’re happy with is safe.

items.text: A hug from Nani that you like
items.explanation: Safe touch feels good and is never secret.

items.text: A doctor’s check-up with Mom in the room
items.explanation: A doctor may need to check you, with a parent there.

items.text: A hug from a relative that you don’t want
items.explanation: You can say, “I’d like a high five instead.” Your body, your choice.

items.text: A friend keeps tickling after you said stop
items.explanation: Stop means stop. Say no firmly, and tell an adult if it continues.

items.text: Someone touches the parts a swimsuit covers
items.explanation: Say NO, GO away, and TELL a trusted adult. It’s never your fault.

items.text: An adult says, “This touch is our little secret”
items.explanation: Touch should never be a secret. Tell someone you trust.

items.text: Someone shows you pictures that make you uncomfortable
items.explanation: That’s not okay. Leave and tell a trusted adult.

outro_steps: TELL a trusted adult, and keep telling

config.instructions: Collect your 6 rights cards. Tap each one to learn what the law promises you.
config.done_line: The law is on your side. You are protected, you will be believed, and help is one call away.

cards.name: Protected till 18
cards.back: POCSO protects every child in India under 18 years.
cards.tip: That includes you, and your friends.

cards.name: Every child
cards.back: Girls, boys, every child is protected the same way.

cards.name: Never your fault
cards.back: Under 18, the law says a child cannot agree to sexual acts. The adult is always responsible.
cards.tip: Even if someone says “you said yes”.

cards.name: Name kept private
cards.back: A child’s name, photo or school can’t be shared in the news.

cards.name: Child-friendly help
cards.back: Special courts and trained officers make it easier to speak. A trusted adult can stay with you.

cards.name: Anyone can report
cards.back: A child, parent, teacher or neighbour can call 1098 or 112, or go to the police.

config.instructions: Is it a green flag (healthy) or a red flag (not okay) in a friendship? Wave the right flag!
config.done_line: Keep the green flags close. For red flags, use your “I feel… when… I need…” words, and talk to a trusted adult.

items.text: Celebrates when you do well
items.explanation: Real friends cheer for you.

items.text: Says sorry after hurting you
items.explanation: Owning mistakes builds trust.

items.text: Respects it when you say no
items.explanation: A no should be accepted, every time.

items.text: Listens when you talk
items.explanation: Feeling heard is a sign of a good friendship.

items.text: Makes fun of you in front of others
items.explanation: Jokes that hurt aren’t jokes.

items.text: Pressures you to do things you don’t want
items.explanation: Good friends never push you.

items.text: Gets angry when you have other friends
items.explanation: You can have many friends.

items.text: Shares your private chats
items.explanation: Breaking trust is a red flag.

review_links.label: The four phases of the cycle

questions.prompt: What is a period?

options.text: The uterus lining leaving the body

questions.explanation: The lining leaves gently, and a new cycle begins.
questions.hint: Think of the cosy lining from the video.

questions.prompt: For most teens, how long is a cycle?
questions.explanation: 21 to 45 days is common for teens.
questions.hint: It’s a few weeks, and can vary.

questions.prompt: Which hormone builds the lining?
questions.explanation: Oestrogen builds it; progesterone keeps it ready.
questions.hint: It rises in the first half of the cycle.

questions.prompt: Which organ releases an egg?
questions.explanation: The ovary releases an egg around the middle of the cycle.
questions.hint: Its name sounds a bit like “oval”.

questions.prompt: What is menarche?
questions.explanation: Menarche is the very first period.
questions.hint: It was the first stamp in your passport story.

questions.prompt: Every girl starts puberty at exactly the same age.
questions.explanation: False. Everyone has her own timing.

questions.prompt: Periods can be irregular in the first year or two.
questions.explanation: True, and that’s completely normal.
questions.hint: Your body is still finding its rhythm.

questions.prompt: How much blood is lost in a whole period, usually?
questions.explanation: Usually just 2 to 3 tablespoons in total.

questions.prompt: Which is a sign to tell a grown-up?

options.text: A period lasting more than 7 days

questions.explanation: Bleeding for more than 7 days is worth checking with a doctor.
questions.hint: Think of the Flow Detective cases.

questions.prompt: Which can delay a period?
questions.explanation: Stress, illness and big weight changes can shift the cycle.

questions.prompt: How often should you change a pad?
questions.explanation: Every 4 to 6 hours, sooner if full.

questions.prompt: Which way should you wipe?
questions.explanation: Front to back keeps germs away.

questions.prompt: What do you need to wash outside the vagina?
questions.explanation: Plain water outside is enough.

questions.prompt: Which products can be reused?
questions.explanation: Cups and cloth pads can be washed and reused.

questions.prompt: A tampon should never stay in longer than…
questions.explanation: 8 hours at most.
questions.hint: Less than one school day plus a bit.

questions.prompt: Pads can be flushed down the toilet.
questions.explanation: False. Wrap and bin.
questions.hint: What did Wrap It Right say?

questions.prompt: Where should cloth pads dry?
questions.explanation: Sunlight helps kill germs.

questions.prompt: What goes in a school-day kit?
questions.explanation: A small pouch keeps you ready.

questions.prompt: Which product works for swimming?
questions.explanation: Pads don’t work in water.

questions.prompt: Periods are something to hide and be ashamed of.
questions.explanation: False! Periods are natural.

questions.prompt: What makes the uterus squeeze during a period?
questions.explanation: Prostaglandins cause the squeezing cramps.

questions.prompt: Which can ease cramps?
questions.explanation: Warmth relaxes the muscles.

questions.prompt: What helps a bloated belly?
questions.explanation: Water and less salt help.

questions.prompt: Pain that makes you miss school every month means…
questions.explanation: Strong pain deserves a doctor’s help.

questions.prompt: Which can be a sign of PCOS?
questions.explanation: A doctor can check and help manage PCOS.

questions.prompt: Menorrhagia means…
questions.explanation: Very heavy or long bleeding.

questions.prompt: Amenorrhea means…
questions.explanation: No periods by 15, or 3 missed in a row.

questions.prompt: Some clear or white discharge is…
questions.explanation: Healthy discharge keeps the vagina clean.

questions.prompt: Itching and thick white discharge can mean…
questions.explanation: A doctor can treat it easily.

questions.prompt: If you notice signs of an infection, you should…

options.text: Tell a grown-up and see a doctor

questions.explanation: Telling is the fastest way to feel better.

extra_unscored.prompt: Who is in your Safe Circle?

questions.prompt: Bullying is…

options.text: Hurting someone again and again on purpose

questions.explanation: Repeated, on purpose and hurtful.
questions.hint: Three parts: again, on purpose, hurts.

questions.prompt: An upstander…

options.text: Helps safely and tells an adult

questions.explanation: Upstanders include, don’t join in, and tell.

questions.prompt: A stranger online asks for your photo. You…
questions.explanation: Never share photos with strangers.

questions.prompt: Private parts are the parts covered by…
questions.explanation: The swimsuit rule.

questions.prompt: No, Go, …
questions.explanation: No, Go, Tell, and keep telling.
questions.hint: The third step is about your Safe Circle.

questions.prompt: What is a period?

options.text: The uterus lining leaving the body

questions.explanation: The lining leaves gently, and a new cycle begins.
questions.hint: Think of the cosy lining from the video.

questions.prompt: What is menarche?
questions.explanation: Menarche is the very first period.

questions.prompt: Which is a sign to tell a grown-up?

options.text: A period lasting more than 7 days

questions.explanation: Bleeding for more than 7 days is worth checking with a doctor.

questions.prompt: How often should you change a pad?
questions.explanation: Every 4 to 6 hours, sooner if full.

questions.prompt: Which products can be reused?

questions.prompt: Pads can be flushed down the toilet.

questions.prompt: What makes the uterus squeeze during a period?

questions.prompt: If you notice signs of an infection, you should…

guardrails: No leaderboards or comparing with other girls
No rewards tied to her body, her period or her diary contents
No paid currency, ads or pressure tactics
Parents see badges and petal totals, never what she bought or wrote
No push notifications to her; reminders go to the parent
No offers or prices in her space

myth_of_the_day_pool.statement: “You shouldn’t exercise or play during your period.”
myth_of_the_day_pool.explanation: Gentle movement often eases cramps. Dance, play, stretch, whatever feels good for you.

myth_of_the_day_pool.statement: “Once your periods start, you stop growing taller.”
myth_of_the_day_pool.explanation: Growth slows down, but most girls still grow a few more centimetres after their first period.

myth_of_the_day_pool.statement: “During your period you’ll spoil pickle if you touch it.”
myth_of_the_day_pool.explanation: Periods can’t spoil food. This belief has no science behind it at all.

myth_of_the_day_pool.statement: “You shouldn’t bathe or wash your hair during your period.”
myth_of_the_day_pool.explanation: A warm bath keeps you fresh and can even ease cramps.

myth_of_the_day_pool.statement: “Girls can’t use tampons or cups until they’re grown up.”
myth_of_the_day_pool.explanation: Teens can use them too, when they feel ready and know how. Many girls start with pads first.

myth_of_the_day_pool.statement: “It’s fine to flush a pad if you’re in a hurry.”
myth_of_the_day_pool.explanation: Pads swell up and block pipes. Always wrap and bin, even in a hurry.
When everyone understands periods, there’s less teasing and more support.

myth_of_the_day_pool.statement: “Pain that makes you miss school every month is just normal.”
myth_of_the_day_pool.explanation: Strong pain is worth checking with a doctor. You don’t have to just put up with it.

myth_of_the_day_pool.statement: “If you have a menstrual disorder, you did something wrong.”
myth_of_the_day_pool.explanation: These conditions are nobody’s fault. Doctors can help you feel better.

myth_of_the_day_pool.statement: “Only girls who aren’t clean get infections.”
myth_of_the_day_pool.explanation: Anyone can get one. Infections are common, treatable and nothing to be ashamed of.

myth_of_the_day_pool.statement: “Telling an adult about bullying is snitching.”
myth_of_the_day_pool.explanation: Telling is getting help. Adults can do things kids can’t.
Sometimes it can be someone a child knows. That’s why every child can say no and tell, about anyone.
Anyone can report, including a child, a parent or a teacher.
Even best friends disagree. What matters is how you sort it out.
Crying is a healthy way to let feelings out. Brave people feel things too.
